titleStmt.title: Simultaneous Optimisation of Task Mapping and Priority Assignment for Real-Time Embedded NoCs

analytic.title: Simultaneous Optimisation of Task Mapping and Priority Assignment for Real-Time Embedded NoCs

div.p: In a hard real-time embedded system based on a fixed priority pre-emptive Networks-On-Chip (NoC), the provision of guaranteed services may require pre-emption of some tasks and messages based on their priorities. In a worst case scenario, the interference imposed to low priority tasks can cause substantial computation and communication delays that can exceed their deadlines, leading to an unschedulable system. In a task mapping optimisation process, changing task mappings does not always produce a schedulable task mapping. In this paper, we propose an approach that simultaneously optimises task mapping and priority assignment, aiming to find a configuration that can completely satisfy the timing constraints of the system. Differing to the state-of-the-art, our approach takes into account the overall schedulability of the system by considering the worstcase end-to-end response time of all mapped tasks. As a result, we are able to increase the quality of task mappings at the same time improving the convergence of the optimisation algorithm, better than the previous approaches that solely focus on the task mapping optimisation to make the system schedulable.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Computing resources are shared differently between tasks depending on a task mapping. As a result, low priority tasks may receive lengthy pre-emptions, which could delay their end-to-end response time to the extent deadline misses occur in the system. If the priority assignment policy [1] is optimal, it can provide a schedulable priority ordering whenever such an ordering exists, but this is not always the case. According to the policy [1], priorities are assigned to tasks based on their minimum inter-arrival interval or period (e.g. from Table I, the priority ordering is τ 1 > τ 2 > τ 3 ). While optimal in a single processor, it limits the way for a NoC based multiprocessor system to become fully schedulable. A task with the longest period, which shares resources with those with short periods, suffers the most interference. For example, in Fig. 1a task τ 3 failed to meet its deadline (assuming it is equivalent to period). On the other hand, if the priority ordering of tasks is changed to τ 2 > τ 1 > τ 3 , as depicted in Fig. 1b not a single task misses its deadline. By changing the priority ordering, the amount of interference received by low priority tasks can be reduced whilst at the same time allowing the high priority tasks to have the needed access on the resources. In this paper, we propose a technique that allows an optimisation algorithm to explore a wide design space. The aim

Rescheduling of tasks and messages to improve response time is to find a task mapping and a priority assignment, which are feasible for the system to execute tasks and to send messages within their timing constraints. This is achieved by relaxing the amount of interference experienced by low priority tasks and messages without sacrificing their high priority counterparts.

In our approach, task mapping and priority assignment are performed simultaneously during the optimisation process to achieve a fully schedulable system. The underlying fitness function that supports the process is based on the end-to-end schedulability analysis. This analysis finds the upper bound of the end-to-end response time and analysed it against the deadline.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In the early work related to fixed priority scheduling on a single-processor system, Liu and Layland [2] introduced the rate monotonic priority assignment policy: the highest priority is given to the task with the shortest period. Based on the same policy, Mutka [3] addressed the scheduling problem of wormhole switching real-time networks. However, this policy cannot be referred as optimal because it does not always find a schedulable priority ordering whenever such an ordering exists. For NoC with wormhole switching, Shi [4] applied the Branch and Bound heuristic to find a schedulable priority ordering for a set of traffic flows, assuming a task mapping is given. However, they did not address the problem of finding a schedulable task mapping or the priority ordering of tasks.

Researchers have considered the end-to-end response time in their approaches using Genetic Algorithm (GA) or other heuristics such as Mixed Integer Linear Programming [5], Branch and Bound [6] and Constraint Programming [7] to address the task mapping and the priority assignment problems for multiple processors. However, those works only focused on bus-based communication, which makes the evaluation model less applicable for NoC based hard real-time systems. Focusing on NoC communication model, other researchers [8], [9] have proposed several task mapping approaches based on the end-toend schedulability analysis. With GAs, they have shown that achieving a schedulable system by solely changing the task mapping is possible. However, in some cases such as when the computing resources are exhausted by too many contending tasks, finding a feasible task mapping on a NoC platform with limited computing and networking resources is difficult.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: An application model describes the design-time characteristics of computation and communication load imposed by an application. Tasks and messages of the application are released either periodically or sporadically. We assume that a task can only transmit a message after its execution and the overhead of the NoC Network Interface is negligible. Therefore, the endto-end response time upper bound of a task that communicates with another task at a different core includes the amount of time since its release until the last packet that it sends arrives at the receiving task in a worst-case scenario. Packetisation of a message before its transmission produces one or several packets. A traffic flow represents a series of packets sent over the NoC from a source task to a destination task. Every task is described as T ask = {c, t, p, d}, where c is the worstcase execution time of task, t is the minimum inter-arrival interval of task, p is the priority level of task and d is the end-to-end deadline of task. Each message is described as Msg = {So, De, P, L, C}, where So is the source task, De is the receiving task, P is the priority level of message, L is the length of message and C is the no-load latency of message. The worst-case execution time (WCET, denoted by variable c i ) is the maximum time that a task can take to finish execution when running on its own over a processing core. Likewise, given a specific path over the NoC and a maximum packet size, the no-load latency of a traffic flow (C i ) is its latency when no traffic-flow contention exists. For most NoCs, the noload latency can be deterministically found and it is a function of the number of hops, the number of flits, the time needed for a flit to traverse a link and the time needed for a router to route and arbitrate packet headers. The platform is modelled to represent the architecture of an on-chip multicore system interconnected with NoC. We implemented the platform as a 2D Mesh with deterministic routing and wormhole switching. The arbitration unit supports flit-level pre-emption to control the access of packets to shared links in accordance with their priorities. A processing core can run more than one task and a link can be shared by multiple traffic flows.

div.head: A. End-to-End Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The proposed simultaneous optimisation technique applies the end-to-end schedulability analysis [10] to determine the schedulability of all tasks and flows in the system. To reduce the complexity of the analysis, we assume the deadline of a task is equivalent to its period (i.e. d = t) and a traffic flow share the same deadline as its sending task. If for each task i of a task set, r i ≤ d i , then the task set is deemed schedulable on the platform, where r i is the worst-case response time and d i is the deadline of task i. If task i is not schedulable, Ut i has value one.

div.p: The release of a traffic flow only occurs after the sending task finishes its execution and the overhead to packetise its payload is negligible. Therefore, each flow's maximum release jitter can be deduced as the worst-case response time (r i ) of the task that releases it. With these assumptions, the end-toend response time of a task is defined as the time taken from its release until the last packet it sends arrives at the receiving task. Traffic flows that are sent to another task at the other core may not be schedulable if they fail to meet the deadline of their sending task (e.g. due to the interference from other packets sharing the same path or to the delay in execution of the task itself). div.head: B. Optimisation Objective & Design Space
div.p: We chose GA as the optimisation algorithm in our approach, as it is widely known for solving optimisation problems. The algorithm is based on evolutionary principles; it produces a group of individuals in a population and evolves them to create better individuals over a number of evolution cycles, or generations. In order to guide the optimisation algorithm the objective function is derived as equation ( 2), where S is given by equation (1). Every individual in the population is a possible configuration for the system, and evolving them requires manipulation of their chromosomes. Each individual's chromosome has the same structure as shown in Fig. 2 and it contains the information of a task mapping and a priority assignment. Small units called genes in the chromosome is divided into two parts to represent this information. The first half of the chromosome (green) represents the task mapping. Each gene in this part carries an integer index value of a processing core onto which the task that it represents will be mapped in the system. A processing core can have more than one tasks mapped onto it, hence the same index (of a processing core) can appear more than one in different genes. For example, task τ 1 (1st gene) and task τ 3 (3rd gene) are mapped onto the same processing core with index five. Priority assignment is encoded in the second part (orange) of the chromosome. In a fixed priority pre-emptive scheduling, it is commonly assumed that priority of every task is unique i.e. the same priority cannot be assigned to more than one task. Therefore, the information in the genes is structured in a way that every task will have a priority different than the others. This is implemented by structuring the genes to represent the sequence of all tasks in getting a priority from a priority set. For example, given a set containing priorities in descending order (i.e. from high to low priority), task τ 3 has value one and hence gets the first turn to receive the highest priority than the rest of the tasks. Task τ 1 with value two gets the second turn, and subsequently followed by the rest of the tasks. When different tasks get the same value, the order of precedence is decided from the left side of the chromosome. For example, task τ 2 and task τ 4 share the same value (three), hence task τ 2 firstly receives a priority followed by task τ 4 i.e. priority of task τ 2 is higher than task τ 4 . Nevertheless, the priority set can be implemented in different orders.

div.head: A. Experimental Setup & Test Benches
div.p: It is relatively easy to achieve 100% schedulability using test benches with low utilisation. Our target is to focus at the boundary where the system will start to become unschedulable at certain levels of utilisation. This is also to keep the number of tests relevant. The test benches were numbered in consecutive numbering proportional to their utilisation levels e.g. TB1 has lower utilisation level than TB5. The total of the test benches is 20 and each test bench constitutes between 46%-73% utilisation of a 5x5 platform. Two kind of priority assignment policies mainly the Rate Monotonic priority assignment [1] (referred as RM) and the random priority assignment (referred as RAN) were used for assigning a priority to each task in the test benches. Every task has a unique priority and a flow inherits the same priority from its sending task. The test benches were mapped onto 4x4 and 5x5 NoC based mesh platforms. To further study the proposed technique with a realistic application, Autonomous Vehicle Application (AVA) test bench was also applied in the experimental work.

The optimisation algorithm combined with the proposed approach is called SCGA and it was compared with more than one baselines. One of the baselines is GA, which only configures task mapping and depends on RM and RAN for assigning a priority to every task. Since SCGA and GA have similar optimisation process, the same optimisation settings from [11] were applied on both of them. GA does not directly configure priority assignment during optimisation, hence its chromosome only contains task mapping, which is similar to the first part of the SCGA's chromosome (Fig. 2). The same technique as [4] based on Branch and Bound (BB) heuristic to address the priority assignment problem of NoC was also used as a baseline. BB was implemented to find a priority assignment for a set of tasks for the best GA(RAN) task mapping that it receives as input.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: The performance of the best task mapping found by SCGA, GA(RM), GA(RAN) and BB on the 4x4 platform is plotted in the graph depicted in Fig. 3a. SCGA outperformed GA(RM), GA(RAN) and BB with its fully schedulable task mapping from TB1 to TB5. From TB6 to TB10, SCGA unable to find any schedulable task mapping for the system but the schedulability percentages are higher than all the baselines. None of the baselines were able to find any schedulable task mapping for all the test benches. Meanwhile, in the 5x5 platform, SCGA and GA(RM) showed similar performance and able to find fully schedulable task mappings for TB5 until TB14, as depicted in Fig. 3b. SCGA maintained the same performance afterwards until TB17, better than GA(RM) that started to show performance drop from TB15. From TB18 until TB20, neither SCGA, GA(RAN), GA(RM) nor BB were able to make the system schedulable, however, SCGA showed higher schedulability percentages than all the baselines. Both GA(RAN) and BB were unable to find any schedulable task mapping for all the test benches except BB with TB11 test bench.

SCGA, GA(RAN) and GA(RM) took certain amount of progress to find the first schedulable task mapping for the system during optimisation. Fig. 4 shows a comparison between the algorithms through the number of generations taken Fig. 4. Progress for finding the first schedulable mapping on a 4x4 platform to find the task mapping. At the maximum generations (500), a schedulable task mapping can be either found or otherwise. In Fig. 3a we have shown that GA(RM) and GA(RAN) were unable to produce any schedulable task mapping for all the test benches, and therefore both algorithms are plotted with the maximum generations. Meanwhile, SCGA progressed better than its counterparts, finding the first feasible task mapping for all the test benches in less than 100 generations, except from TB6 to TB10 where it failed to find any schedulable task mapping. We have discussed hitherto, the feasibility of SCGA in improving the task mapping and priority assignment based on synthetic test benches. To further demonstrate the feasibility of SCGA, it was used to map a realistic test bench (AVA) on the 4x4 platform. As depicted in Fig. 5, SCGA, GA(RM) and GA(RAN) achieved the same result, all of them converged to a schedulable task mapping. However, with faster converging rate below 30 generations SCGA proved it is better than its counterparts that took more than 100 generations to converge. Simultaneous configuration of task mapping and priority assignment technique enables SCGA to become an efficient exploration tool. In spite of an additional dimension above the existing task mapping configuration, the algorithm still able to improve the schedulability of the system without affecting much on the optimisation progress.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: A task mapping is not feasible for a hard real-time embedded system if the system becomes unschedulable due to the interference suffered by low priority tasks. Reducing the interference is possible by changing the priority assignment of the mapped tasks to lessen the effects of pre-emption when sharing the same resources. Based on this notion, we proposed an approach that configures both task mapping and priority assignment, which can be used by GA-based optimisation algorithm to find a feasible configuration for the system. Finding the configuration considers the overall schedulability of every task and message by taking into account the endto-end response time. From the experimental results, we were able to find the configuration for synthetic and realistic test benches on different platforms, better than the baselines. In future work, we will explore additional design spaces such as routing and lift some of the restrictions to allow validation of messages with the same priority.
